The fence 30 is a fixed fence, by which is meant that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and is not slidable along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below are. No setting of the jig is made by moving the fence 30 along the rail 10, and no position along the length of the rail 10 other than the first end is available to it. A fixed fence in this sense is not a permanent one. As described below, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the rail 10 and may be taken off and reinstalled in either of two orientations, and it occupies the same fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 in both of those orientations. 9	Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. The fence 30 is securable in a second orientation upon removal of the two screws 34, inversion of the fence 30, and reinstallation of the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36, and in that second orientation the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. 22

The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe from the lower face 14 and permits the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80 are each disposed below the lower face 14 of the rail 10 and bear against the lower face 14 when the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 respectively are tightened, and each is released from the lower face 14 when the clamp knob of its guide carriage is loosened.
24	
25	The first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82, as seen in FIG. 2. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is an index feature that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.
26

28

The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 7) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, for alignment with a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 7) drawn on the workpiece 90. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 are aligned with one another, and the user aligns the transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 with the centerline 94 before drilling.
30

The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair relative to the centerline 94. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 are aligned with the centerline 94.
32	
33	A method of locating and guiding the pair of holes with the jig is carried out as follows. The user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.
34	
35	The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. Where an increased setback is wanted, the spacer plate 40 is fitted between the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the workpiece edge 92 before the downwardly projecting portion 32 is pressed against that edge. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which fixes the setback. The sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are then aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.
36	
37	When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, after the jig has been lifted away from the workpiece 90, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.
38	
39	The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushing 54 and the drill bushing 74 are made of hardened metal.
40	
41	The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. It is held against the front face of the workpiece 90 by hand during the drilling, and no part of it remains attached to the workpiece 90. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.
42	
43	The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.
